props.title: Heaven Can Wait
props.initialSlug: Devil tempts playboy with scandalous life review

sections.content: Ernst Lubitsch's Heaven Can Wait masterfully blends comedy and melancholy in ways that influenced romantic cinema for decades. The story of Henry Van Cleve (Don Ameche) pleading his case to enter Hell showcases Lubitsch's famous "touch" - that ineffable mix of sophistication, wit, and grace. It's fascinating to compare this with other afterlife comedies like Here Comes Mr. Jordan (1941) and A Matter of Life and Death (1946), which similarly use the heaven/hell framework to explore human nature, but with distinctly different tones.

sections.content: The film's innovative structure - using the framing device of a posthumous confession - influenced later works like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and American Beauty (1999), where deceased narrators reflect on their lives. Lubitsch's signature style shines through in the delicate handling of marital infidelity and family dynamics, treating potentially scandalous material with sophisticated humor rather than judgment. The Technicolor photography by Edward Cronjager creates a warm, nostalgic glow that perfectly captures the film's wistful tone.

What sets Heaven Can Wait apart from contemporary Hollywood comedies is its mature approach to romance and mortality. Unlike the screwball comedies of the era like The Lady Eve (1941) or The Palm Beach Story (1942), Lubitsch takes a gentler, more philosophical approach. The film's influence can be seen in later works like Defending Your Life (1991) and The Good Place (2016-2020), which similarly use the afterlife as a lens to examine human behavior. sections.content: The sophisticated dialogue and subtle innuendo that characterize Heaven Can Wait established a template for intelligent romantic comedy that echoes through films like The Shop Around the Corner (1940) and even modern classics like When Harry Met Sally (1989). Lubitsch's ability to suggest rather than show, to imply rather than state, created a new language for depicting romance on screen that continues to influence filmmakers today.
